source.title: The Richest Man in Babylon
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of The Richest Man in Babylon by George S. Clason (1926). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Public domain in the US since 2022, but in copyright until the end of 2027 in life+70 countries (the author died in 1957), so cards are original summaries without quotes.

cards.title: Keep a slice of everything you earn before you spend any of it
cards.body:
The book's central lesson, told through parables set in ancient Babylon, is that wealth starts when you treat part of every income as yours to keep. Clason's characters set aside at least one coin in ten before paying for anything else.

The point is the order. If saving waits until the bills and treats are covered, there is rarely anything left. Taken off the top, a tenth is small enough that you barely miss it, yet over years it grows into real security. Today that looks like an automatic transfer to savings on payday.
cards.apply_it: Set up an automatic transfer of 10% (or whatever you can start with) into a separate savings account on the day you are paid.

quiz.question: When does the book say you should set aside your savings?
options: Before spending anything else from your income
Only when you get a bonus
At the end of each year
quiz.explanation: Saving first, rather than saving what is left over, is what makes the habit stick.

cards.title: Spending rises to match income unless you separate needs from wants
cards.body:
Clason observes that what people call their necessary expenses tends to grow to fill whatever they earn. A pay rise rarely feels like more money for long, because new wants quietly become "needs".

His remedy is to look honestly at where money goes and sort it: what you genuinely require, and what you simply desire. Desires are endless, so you cannot satisfy them all; you choose the ones worth paying for and let the rest go. A simple budget makes those choices deliberate instead of accidental.
cards.apply_it: Go through last month's spending and mark each item as a need or a want. Pick one want to cut or reduce this month.

quiz.question: What does Clason say tends to happen to 'necessary expenses'?
options: They shrink as you get older
They stay fixed regardless of income
They grow to match whatever you earn
quiz.explanation: Without a deliberate budget, wants creep in and expenses expand to swallow any income.

cards.title: Put your savings to work so they earn more money for you
cards.body:
Saved money sitting idle only protects you. Clason's wealthy characters go a step further: they lend or invest their savings so it produces its own income, and then they reinvest that income too.

The image is of money as a worker that brings back more workers. Each return adds to the pile that earns the next return, so growth speeds up over time. That is the idea of compounding, and it rewards starting early and leaving earnings to build rather than spending them as they arrive.
cards.apply_it: Check where your savings currently sit. If it earns little or nothing, research one low-cost, diversified option where it could grow over time.

quiz.question: Why does the book urge you to reinvest what your savings earn?
options: So that returns build on returns and growth speeds up
quiz.explanation: Reinvested earnings join the pile that produces the next round of earnings: compounding.

cards.title: Protect your savings by taking advice only from people who know the field
cards.body:
One of the book's warnings is that losing money is easier than making it. In a memorable parable, a man entrusts his savings to a brickmaker to buy jewels abroad, and the brickmaker is cheated with worthless glass. The lesson: why ask someone about a trade they have never practised?

Before committing money, Clason advises, make sure the principal is safe and seek counsel from people with real experience in that kind of investment. Tempting promises of fast, large returns deserve extra suspicion. Today this applies to tips from friends, social media hype and anything you do not understand.
cards.apply_it: Before your next financial decision, ask yourself: has the person advising me actually done this successfully, and could I afford to lose this money?

quiz.question: In the brickmaker parable, what went wrong?
options: The jewels were stolen on the road
He trusted someone with no experience in jewels, who was cheated
quiz.explanation: The saver asked for help from someone outside the trade; the lesson is to seek advice from people who know the field.

cards.title: Pay off debts with a fixed share of income while still saving
cards.body:
In one tale, a man deep in debt climbs out with a simple split of every earning: a small portion kept as savings, a larger portion divided among his creditors, and the rest to live on. He explains the plan to the people he owes, and pays each of them a little, regularly, until the debts are gone.

The wisdom still holds. Facing creditors honestly beats hiding from them, steady payments add up, and keeping some savings even while repaying stops you from sliding straight back into borrowing.
cards.apply_it: List every debt you have. Decide a fixed percentage of each payday that goes to repayments, and keep a small amount going to savings as well.

quiz.question: How did the indebted man in the story escape his debts?
options: By borrowing more to pay them off
By ignoring creditors until they gave up
By paying them a regular share of income while saving and living on the rest
By selling everything he owned at once
quiz.explanation: A fixed split between savings, repayments and living costs let him clear his debts steadily.

cards.title: Grow your earning power by getting better at your work
cards.body:
Saving and investing matter, but Clason also stresses the source of it all: your ability to earn. The more skill and knowledge you bring to your work, the more value you can offer, and the more you can reasonably ask to be paid.

His characters study their trades, learn from those ahead of them and take pride in doing work well. The modern version is treating your own skills as an investment: courses, practice, mentors and taking on harder responsibilities all compound into higher income over a career.
cards.apply_it: Name one skill that would make you noticeably more valuable at work. Block an hour this week to start learning it.

quiz.question: According to the book, what underlies all lasting wealth-building?
options: Increasing your own ability to earn
quiz.explanation: Better skills raise the value you offer, which is the root of rising income.

cards.title: Plan now for the years when you can no longer earn
cards.body:
Clason points out that working life does not last forever, and that people who ignore this end up dependent on others. A wise person sets money aside so that income keeps coming in old age, and so their family is cared for if they die early.

He also suggests owning your home rather than paying rent forever, as a way to turn a regular cost into something of value. Today the same thinking points to pensions, retirement accounts and life insurance where it fits your situation.
cards.apply_it: Find out how much you are currently putting toward retirement. If it is nothing, set up even a small regular contribution this month.

quiz.question: Why does the book urge you to provide for the future?
options: Because earning years are limited and family may depend on you
So you can stop saving today
quiz.explanation: Income from work eventually stops, so preparing early protects you and those who depend on you.

cards.title: Hard work alone won't make you secure; learn how money works
cards.body:
The book opens with Bansir, a skilled chariot builder, and his friend Kobbi, a musician. Both have worked hard for years, yet their purses are empty. Their childhood friend Arkad has become the richest man in the city. Their conclusion is that they never learned the rules that govern keeping and growing money.

Clason's message is hopeful: those rules can be learned by anyone. Effort earns money, but knowledge decides whether any of it stays with you. Many diligent people stay poor not from laziness but because no one taught them.
cards.apply_it: Write down one money rule you follow without knowing why. Spend 15 minutes checking whether it actually serves you.

quiz.question: Why did Bansir and Kobbi have nothing despite years of work?
options: They never learned the rules of keeping and growing money
They earned too little to save
quiz.explanation: Clason's point is that effort earns money, but knowledge decides whether it stays.

cards.title: Instead of envying successful people, ask them how they did it
cards.body:
Rather than resenting Arkad's wealth, Bansir and Kobbi gather friends and go to ask him how he became rich. Arkad gladly explains, and his answers form the core of the book.

Clason uses this to show a better response to someone else's success. Envy leaves you where you are; curiosity opens a door. Many people who have built something are willing to share what they learned if asked respectfully. The question is whether you'll swallow your pride and ask.
cards.apply_it: Identify one person who has done well at something you want to improve. Ask them one specific question about how they got started.

quiz.question: How do Bansir and Kobbi respond to Arkad's wealth?
options: They try to borrow from him
They go to ask him how he did it
quiz.explanation: Curiosity, not envy, leads them to the lessons that change their lives.

cards.title: Aim for a steady stream of income, not just a pile of cash
cards.body:
Arkad explains that true wealth is not the coins you carry today but the income that keeps flowing in, even when you aren't working for it. A full purse soon empties if nothing refills it.

This shifts the goal from collecting a lump sum to building sources that keep paying, such as savings that earn interest, a business or skills that keep earning. The question becomes: what will still be bringing money in next year, and the year after?
cards.apply_it: List every source of money that comes to you. Mark which would continue if you stopped working for a month.

quiz.question: How does Arkad describe real wealth?
options: A large pile of gold coins
A steady stream of income that keeps flowing
quiz.explanation: A pile can be spent; a flowing income keeps refilling your purse.

cards.title: Start saving now, even if the amount is tiny
cards.body:
Arkad compares wealth to a tree that grows from a tiny seed. The first coins you save are that seed. The sooner you plant it, the sooner it can grow, and the more care you give it, the bigger it becomes.

Many people wait until they earn more before saving, but Clason's image suggests the opposite. The habit and the head start matter more than the first amount. A small sum saved today begins growing years before a larger sum saved 'someday'.
cards.apply_it: Move the smallest amount you won't miss into savings today. The point is to plant the seed, not the size of it.

quiz.question: What image does Arkad use to describe how wealth grows?
options: A house built in a day
A tree growing from a small seed
quiz.explanation: Wealth starts small, like a seed, and grows over time when planted early.

cards.title: Expect to stumble while learning to save, and start again
cards.body:
Arkad admits he didn't get it right at first. His early savings were lost when he trusted the wrong person with them. Later, when his savings did earn something, he spent the earnings on fine clothes and feasts instead of letting them grow. His mentor scolded him both times.

Only on his third attempt did the lessons stick. Clason shows that even the richest man in Babylon learned through failure. Mistakes don't mean you're bad with money; quitting after them is what keeps you stuck.
cards.apply_it: Recall a money mistake you made. Write the lesson in one line, then take one small step to restart.

quiz.question: What happened in Arkad's early attempts to build wealth?
options: He lost savings and then spent his earnings before learning
quiz.explanation: Arkad failed twice before succeeding, showing that setbacks are part of learning.

cards.title: Build willpower by keeping small promises to yourself
cards.body:
Arkad explains that willpower is simply the firm intention to finish what you set out to do. He says that if he set himself even a trivial task, such as throwing a pebble into the river every day for a hundred days, he would complete it. Otherwise, he reasons, he could never trust himself with the bigger ones.

This is a practical idea. Each small commitment you keep builds confidence that you'll keep the next. It's also wise to avoid setting tasks so hard or unclear that you're likely to abandon them.
cards.apply_it: Choose a tiny daily task for the next 30 days, such as saving a coin. Keep it, and notice how your self-trust grows.

quiz.question: How does Arkad build his willpower?
options: By keeping even small promises to himself
quiz.explanation: Keeping small commitments trains you to trust yourself with bigger ones.

cards.title: Turn vague wishes into specific goals
cards.body:
Clason distinguishes between a general wish and a definite desire. Wanting 'to be rich' is too vague to act on. Wanting to save a specific amount, then a larger one, gives you something concrete to work toward.

He suggests starting with modest, clear targets. Reaching a small one builds the ability and confidence to set the next. Over time a series of achievable goals can take you much further than one huge, fuzzy dream.
cards.apply_it: Rewrite one vague money wish, like 'save more', as a specific target with an amount and a date.

quiz.question: What does Clason say about wishes versus desires?
options: Specific, definite desires are stronger than vague wishes
quiz.explanation: Concrete, achievable targets give you a clear path; vague wishes don't.

cards.title: Learn how to find out what you don't know
cards.body:
Arkad describes two kinds of learning. One is the knowledge you already have: facts and skills you've studied. The other is the ability to discover what you don't yet know: knowing whom to ask, where to look and how to test an idea.

The second kind matters more as the world changes. You can't know everything about money or work, but you can get good at finding reliable information and learning from people with experience.
cards.apply_it: Next time you face a money question you can't answer, write down three places or people you could reliably learn from.

quiz.question: What are Arkad's two kinds of learning?
options: What you already know, and the skill of finding out what you don't
quiz.explanation: Knowing how to learn new things is as valuable as what you already know.

cards.title: Good luck tends to find people who act on opportunities
cards.body:
In one chapter, a group of Babylonians discuss how to attract good luck. They tell stories of chances they let slip because they hesitated, and conclude that what looks like luck usually comes to people who are prepared and willing to act.

Clason's point is that opportunity rarely waits. Having savings, skills and an open mind puts you in a position to say yes when the right chance appears, while others are still thinking about it.
cards.apply_it: Think of an opportunity you missed by waiting. Write what preparation would have let you act, and start on it.

quiz.question: According to the Babylonians' discussion, who tends to get good luck?
options: People who are prepared and act on opportunities
People born in the right family
quiz.explanation: Luck often favours those who are ready and willing to act.

cards.title: Notice your habit of putting decisions off
cards.body:
In the same discussion about luck, the characters admit that the real obstacle was often inside themselves: a habit of delay. A good deal would appear, they would decide to think about it, and by the time they returned it was gone.

Clason presents procrastination as an enemy that must be recognised before it can be beaten. This doesn't mean acting rashly. It means doing your homework and then deciding, rather than letting a vague 'later' make the choice for you.
cards.apply_it: Pick one decision you've been postponing. Set a deadline this week, gather what you need and decide by then.

quiz.question: What do Clason's characters identify as their real obstacle to luck?
quiz.explanation: Procrastination caused them to miss chances that others took.

cards.title: Gambling is a poor path to wealth
cards.body:
When Clason's characters ask whether luck can be found at the gaming tables or the races, they agree it can't be counted on. The people who reliably profit from gambling are those who run it, because the odds are set in their favour.

The point still holds today with betting apps, lotteries and casinos. An occasional win can feel like luck, but over time most players lose. Wealth built through saving, work and careful investing is far more dependable.
cards.apply_it: Add up what you've spent on betting or lotteries in the past year, if anything. Decide what you could do with that amount instead.

quiz.question: Who tends to profit from gambling, according to Clason's characters?
quiz.explanation: The odds favour the house, so gamblers lose over time.

cards.title: Before lending money, ask how it will be repaid
cards.body:
In one story, a spearmaker named Rodan receives a gift of gold, and his sister asks him to lend it to her husband for a new business. Rodan seeks advice from a gold lender, who shows him a box of keepsakes from past loans. Loans backed by something solid, or given to people who could clearly repay, came back. Loans given out of sympathy to people with no plan often did not.

The lesson is not to stop helping others, but to lend with open eyes. Ask what the money is for, whether the borrower understands that venture and how they will repay.
cards.apply_it: Before your next loan to anyone, write down how and when it will be repaid. If that's unclear, consider a smaller gift instead.

quiz.question: What did the gold lender's box of keepsakes teach Rodan?
options: Lend with care, considering how repayment will happen
Lending is the fastest way to get rich
quiz.explanation: Loans backed by security or a clear plan were repaid; sympathy loans often weren't.

cards.title: Help others in ways that don't make their burden yours
cards.body:
Rodan's story continues with a broader lesson about family and money. A sudden windfall brought requests from relatives, and he felt pressure to say yes. The gold lender's advice was that if you want to help someone, do it in a way that doesn't drag you down with them.

This is a healthy boundary, not selfishness. Lending money you can't afford to lose, or funding a plan that is likely to fail, can damage both your finances and the relationship. Sometimes the kindest help is advice, a smaller gift or helping someone build a skill.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you want to help financially. Decide what amount you could give or lend without harming your own stability.

quiz.question: What advice did the gold lender give Rodan about helping others?
options: Help in a way that doesn't take their burdens on yourself
quiz.explanation: Helping wisely protects both you and the relationship.

cards.title: Build your defences before trouble arrives
cards.body:
In one short chapter, an old warrior guards a gate of Babylon while an enemy army attacks. The people are frightened, but the city's great walls hold. Clason draws a lesson from it: people need protection against unexpected disasters, and the time to build it is before the attack.

Today those walls might be an emergency fund, health cover, insurance where it makes sense, or simply avoiding risks that could ruin you. They feel unnecessary in calm times, but they let you get through the storm when it comes.
cards.apply_it: List one financial 'wall' you lack, such as an emergency fund. Take one small step to start building it this month.

quiz.question: What lesson does Clason draw from the walls of Babylon?
options: Protection must be built before disaster strikes
Walls are a waste of money
quiz.explanation: The walls held because they were built in advance, like financial safeguards.

cards.title: Where there is real determination, a way can be found
cards.body:
Dabasir, a camel trader, tells how he fell from comfort into debt, fled his city and was enslaved. After much hardship, he made up his mind to return and face what he owed. He says that once his determination was firm, he found ways forward that he hadn't seen before.

Clason's point is that circumstances matter, but so does resolve. A firm decision focuses your attention and energy, and options start to appear. Many problems look impossible until you truly commit to solving them.
cards.apply_it: Name one problem you've been half-heartedly trying to fix. Write down a firm decision about it and one first step.

quiz.question: What lesson does Dabasir draw from his journey?
options: Determination helps you find a way forward
quiz.explanation: Once he truly committed, he found paths he hadn't seen before.

cards.title: Face your obligations with self-respect instead of running from them
cards.body:
While enslaved, Dabasir is challenged with a question: does he have the soul of a free man or of a slave? Clason uses it to describe two mindsets. One makes excuses and runs from problems; the other takes responsibility, faces difficulties and works to set them right.

For Dabasir, that meant going home to repay his debts honestly. The book treats this not as a moral lecture but as a source of strength. Taking ownership of your obligations restores self-respect, and that self-respect makes the hard work possible.
cards.apply_it: Write down one obligation you've been avoiding. Decide on one honest step to face it this week.

quiz.question: What does the 'soul of a free man' represent in Dabasir's story?
quiz.explanation: It represents ownership of one's problems rather than running from them.

cards.title: Borrowing to live beyond your means can spiral
cards.body:
Dabasir's troubles began when he bought fine things on credit that his earnings couldn't support. When repayments came due he borrowed more, and when he couldn't keep up he fled, which led to far worse trouble.

The lesson is that debt for consumption is easy to start and hard to stop. Today buy-now-pay-later, payday loans and store credit can create the same pattern. Living within your means isn't just about thrift; it keeps you from losing control of your choices.
cards.apply_it: List any debt you carry for things you've already used up. Pick the smallest and plan to clear it first.

quiz.question: How did Dabasir's troubles begin?
options: He bought things on credit he couldn't afford
He gave all his money away
quiz.explanation: Borrowing to fund a lifestyle beyond his means led to deeper debt.

cards.title: Treat work as a friend rather than an enemy
cards.body:
In the final story, Sharru Nada, a rich merchant who was once enslaved, recalls a fellow captive named Megiddo, a farmer, who told him that hard work was the best friend he had ever known. Megiddo urged him to work well for whoever bought him, since that was how he could win respect and, in time, freedom.

The story is told with the cruelty of slavery clearly in view, but its message is about attitude in hard circumstances. Approaching work as a source of skill and pride, rather than something to dodge, built a path forward.
cards.apply_it: Think about a task you resent. Find one way it builds a skill you value, and focus on that next time you do it.

quiz.question: What did Megiddo tell Sharru Nada about work?
options: It was the best friend he had known
quiz.explanation: Megiddo saw work as a source of pride and progress, even in captivity.

cards.title: Look for ways to create extra value from what you already do
cards.body:
Sharru Nada is bought by a baker. He learns the trade quickly and proposes baking honey cakes to sell in the streets, sharing the profits with the baker. With his share he starts saving toward his freedom.

Clason uses this to show initiative: spotting a way your existing skills can earn a little more, and proposing it in a way that benefits others too. Small enterprise, started where you are, can grow into something much bigger.
cards.apply_it: List one skill you use daily. Brainstorm one way it could earn a small extra income or add value to your employer.

quiz.question: How did Sharru Nada begin saving toward his freedom?
options: By selling honey cakes he baked
quiz.explanation: He turned a newly learned skill into extra income through initiative.

cards.title: Wealth you didn't build is easily wasted without the habit of work
cards.body:
Sharru Nada travels with Hadan Gula, the young grandson of his old partner. Hadan wears jewellery, looks down on work and believes it is only for slaves. Sharru Nada tells him that his grandfather was himself once enslaved and built the family fortune through hard work.

Hearing the story changes Hadan's attitude, and he resolves to start humbly as his grandfather did. Clason's point is that money without the skills and values that created it rarely lasts. What a family can truly pass on includes the habits, not just the gold.
cards.apply_it: Think of one money habit you learned from family. Decide whether it is one you want to pass on.

quiz.question: What changed Hadan Gula's attitude toward work?
options: Learning that his grandfather built the fortune through hard work
quiz.explanation: Learning his grandfather's story showed him that wealth came from work.

cards.title: Show you can handle a little before taking on a lot
cards.body:
Arkad tells how he gave his son Nomasir a bag of gold and a clay tablet of advice, then sent him away to prove he could manage money before inheriting the estate. Nomasir quickly lost much of the gold through bad choices before he learned to follow the advice and returned with more than he started with.

The idea is to earn trust with small amounts first. Whether you're managing a first salary, a small business or a family budget, handling modest sums well builds the skill and judgement needed for larger ones.
cards.apply_it: Choose one small budget to manage carefully for a month, such as a food or transport allowance, and review how you did.

quiz.question: Why did Arkad send his son away with a bag of gold?
options: To prove he could manage money before inheriting more
quiz.explanation: Nomasir had to show he could handle a little before being trusted with a lot.

cards.title: Make clear plans for your property in case you die
cards.body:
Among Arkad's advice for protecting your family is to make a proper record of how your property should be divided after your death. Without one, he notes, loved ones may face confusion, unfairness or conflict.

This remains practical today. Depending on your country, a written will, clear records of accounts and named beneficiaries can save your family stress and costs at a painful time. It's a small task that many people delay for years.
cards.apply_it: Write down where your important documents and accounts are, and tell a trusted person where to find the list.

quiz.question: Why does Arkad recommend recording how your property should be divided?
options: To protect your family from confusion and conflict
quiz.explanation: A clear record helps ensure a fair, orderly division for your family.
